problem:
The moment of inertia of a plane lamina of mass $6\,\text{kg}$ about the perpendicular line passing through its center of mass is $4\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$
If the moment of inertia of the same lamina about another perpendicular line is $7\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2},$ find the distance between the two lines.

feedback.problem:
A rectangular plate occupies the region
$D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le 1}$
and has mass density function $\lambda (x,y)=4xy,$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters. The moment of inertia of the plate about a line $l$ perpendicular to the plate is $\frac{16}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$
Given that the center of mass of the plate is at $(2,\frac{2}{3}),$ find the distance of the line $l$ from the center of mass.
feedback.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

First, we find the mass of the plate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}4xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{3}x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{1}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\,{|}_{0}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{9}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =9\,\text{kg}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass $(2,\frac{2}{3})$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}((x-\overset{―}{x})^{2}+(y-\overset{―}{y})^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}((x-2)^{2}+{(y-\frac{2}{3})}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}((x-2)^{2}+{(y-\frac{2}{3})}^{2})\cdot 4xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}x(x-2)^{2}y+x{y}^{3}-\frac{4}{3}x{y}^{2}+\frac{4}{9}xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{2}x(x-2)^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{4}-\frac{4}{9}x{y}^{3}+\frac{2}{9}x{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}x(x-2)^{2}+\frac{1}{4}x-\frac{4}{9}x+\frac{2}{9}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+\frac{73}{36}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{[\frac{1}{8}{x}^{4}-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+\frac{73}{72}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =4(\frac{81}{8}-18+\frac{73}{8}) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{5}{4} \\  & =5\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem and solving for $d,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\ \frac{16}{3} & =5+9{d}^{2} \\ 9{d}^{2} & =\frac{1}{3} \\ {d}^{2} & =\frac{1}{27} \\ d & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}} \\ d & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{9}\,\text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$
